turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Hi. Well, I guess what brings me in is that I just can't seem to shake this heavy mix of fear and guilt. I'm basically tense all day, just... waiting for something else to go wrong. And I keep blaming myself for not stopping what happened.

turns.doctor_question: Can you tell me about what happened that led to these feelings of fear and guilt? Was there a particular event or situation that started all of this?
turns.patient_response: Yeah. All of this started about four months ago. We were doing a porch repair at our house, and... well, my husband fell. It was a bad fall. And this has just been going on ever since that happened.

But I guess the fear and the guilt, being tense all the time... it feels like it's just been there since that day. I don't remember exactly when it settled in, but it hasn't really left since then.

symptom_reasoning.S074: The patient confirms experiencing ongoing fear and guilt that have persistently remained since the day of her husband's fall, meeting criteria for a persistent negative emotional state.

turns.doctor_question: Since your husband's fall, have you been having unwanted memories or flashbacks of what happened? Or do you find yourself reliving the event, even when you don't want to?

Yeah, I do. With my job as a building inspector, I'm around construction sites a lot, so... I'll just be doing something normal, like measuring a railing, or I'll hear a ladder scrape against a wall. And out of nowhere, I can see him falling. 

It's like it's happening right in front of me all over again. My stomach just drops, and my hands start getting shaky. So, yes, the memories definitely come back even when I really don't want them to.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient explicitly confirms experiencing intrusive memories and vivid, flashback-like re-experiencing of her husband's fall triggered by trauma-related cues, accompanied by physiological distress.

turns.doctor_question: Besides those moments when the memories come back unexpectedly, have you been deliberately avoiding things—like avoiding construction sites, or maybe avoiding going near porches or ladders—because they remind you of your husband's fall?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I have. I mean, at work, I've actually started turning down jobs if they involve raised porches or second-story decks. I just pass them on to someone else if I can. symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly confirms avoiding work involving raised porches or decks, avoiding conversations about the repair, and avoiding the physical area where the traumatic accident occurred.

turns.doctor_question: Have you noticed that you're more easily startled than you used to be—like if someone taps you on the shoulder or a door slams, you jump more than normal? Or do you find yourself constantly on edge, scanning your surroundings?

symptom_reasoning.S080: The patient clearly denies an exaggerated startle response, noting they are not more jumpy, loud noises do not bother them more than usual, and they are not easily startled.
